# One Reusable Policy, Not Per-Project

**Decision.** Maintain **one** privacy policy in its own repository, written to be copied and edited
for any project, instead of writing a bespoke policy inside each project that needs one.

**Date.** Stated in the expanded README committed 2026-07-10. Confirmed at interview, 2026-07-28:
"A template, and Pages is live."

## Why

The intent is declared in the first paragraph the reader sees:

> "that does not run analytics, ads, or trackers, and is designed to be **reused** as a template for"
> — privacy-policy/README.md, 2026-07-10

and the policy text itself repeats it, so the reuse claim survives being copied away from the README:

> "and to be reusable across the projects
> maintained by the author."
> — privacy-policy/PRIVACY_POLICY.md, 2026-07-10

Writing privacy law is the expensive part; the per-project delta is usually four fields. So the repo
supplies a checklist of exactly those four — owner name and contact, effective date, the hosting
section, and the cookies/analytics sections — under a "Reuse it for another project" heading. That
list is the decision made operational.

## What it covers today: nothing else in the corpus

This is the finding that matters, and it is chronological. `privacy-policy` was created 2026-02-28
and its full text landed 2026-07-10. [[farely]]'s first commit is 2026-07-12; [[stickfps]]'s is
2026-07-24. **The template predates both by roughly 4.5 and 5 months, so it covers neither.**

The content agrees independently. Farely is an Android app with an accessibility service, on-device
inference, an optional cloud-vision path and a third-party events feed — and it carries its own
privacy documentation that never links here. Stickfps has accounts and a database. The policy
discloses only host server logs and inbound email, "None set by this Service by default" for
cookies, and no other processor. Two independent lines of evidence: `confidence: high`.

So the template is real and the reuse workflow is real, but as of the last commit it is being
applied to **one** thing — the author's own GitHub Pages presence — not to a portfolio of products.

## Alternatives rejected

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **A policy file inside each project** | duplicates the legal text N times; a fix to one never reaches the others |
| **No policy at all** | the author chose to publish one before any product needed it — creation predates every product repo |
| **A generated policy from a service** | no vendor, no generator, no dependency anywhere in the repo — consistent with [[zero-dependency-no-build-step]] |

## The standing risk

A template's factual claims are only true of the deployment it was written for. Applied unedited to
a project with analytics, a database or a cloud API, §6's "does not set its own cookies" and §7's
"No other third-party processors" become **false statements in a legal document** — the worst kind
of drift, because nothing in the file changed. The README's four-field checklist is the mitigation
and is the reason [[controller-vs-processor]] flags §7 as the section that moves.

The mechanism is ordinary [[documentation-drift]] with unusually high stakes; the current state is
safe only because the policy currently describes exactly one site, which is exactly what it says it
describes. See [[host-on-github-pages]] and [[data-minimisation]] for why the unedited defaults are
so absolute in the first place.
